query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloys, applied mechanical stress induces localized amorphization at or near grain boundaries, which forms an ultra‐nanocrystalline surface layer that retards dislocation motion and enhances both hardness and strength (as evidenced by an inverse Hall–Petch effect).
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) in an as-fabricated state with controlled grain sizes ranging from coarse to nanocrystalline.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled mechanical deformation (such as quasi-static compression or sliding wear tests) to samples with systematically varied initial grain sizes under inert conditions.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted in an oxidation-free (ultra-high vacuum or inert atmosphere) environment with uniform sample chemistry; grain sizes and deformation parameters precisely controlled.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary regions that dynamically transform into an amorphous or ultra-nanocrystalline phase during deformation.
generation.mechanism: Under stress, localized high strains and potential thermal effects at grain boundaries trigger a crystalline-to-amorphous transition. This transformation creates an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer that impedes further dislocation movement, resulting in increased resistance to shear and wear. In samples with suitably fine grains, the effect is more pronounced, leading to an inverse Hall–Petch behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical deformation conditions, samples with finer (nanocrystalline) initial grain sizes will exhibit the formation of a near-surface amorphous layer, leading to increased hardness and reduced friction relative to coarse-grained samples.
generation.baseline: Samples with larger grain sizes that show little or no stress-induced amorphization and which obey classical Hall–Petch behavior with lower hardness and wear resistance under similar test conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in single-phase high-entropy alloys under inert conditions where oxidation effects are minimized. In multiphase systems or environments where oxidation occurs, other mechanisms (such as oxide layer formation) may dominate the mechanical response.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical grain size and the chemical compositional effects that control the onset of amorphization remain uncertain and may vary between different HEA systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HEA samples with controlled and well-characterized grain sizes. Subject them to identical controlled mechanical deformations (e.g., compression tests or wear cycles) in an inert atmosphere. Post-deformation, use high-resolution electron microscopy (e.g., STEM) to inspect for the presence of an amorphous or ultra-nanocrystalline layer at grain boundaries. In parallel, measure hardness and friction outcomes.
measurements: Grain size distributions before and after deformation
TEM/STEM imaging for phase characterization at grain boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with fine grains do not exhibit the formation of amorphous or ultra-nanocrystalline layers at the grain boundaries during deformation, or if the hardness and friction metrics do not significantly differ from those in coarse-grained samples, then the hypothesis that stress-induced localized amorphization governs hardness and strength in these HEAs is falsified.

Phase-transition assisted mechanical behavior of TiZrHfTax high-entropy alloys

Abstract: Recent developments of high-entropy alloys with high strength and high ductility draw attention to the metastability-engineering strategy. Using first-principle theory, here we demonstrate that reducing the Ta level in the refractory TiZrHfTax system destabilizes the body-centered cubic (bcc) phase and leads to the appearance of the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phase embedded in the bcc matrix. The alloying-induced features of the elastic parameters for the cubic and hexagonal structures are mapped out in details, and strong sensitivity to the crystal lattice and chemistry is revealed. Results show softening of the bcc matrix with decreasing Ta concentration which ensures ductile behavior. However, the elastically nearly isotropic hcp precipitates possess enhanced resistance against shear which promotes strengthening of the TiZrHfTax dual-phase system. The present atomic-level insight provides strong evidence to the experimental observation, and emphasizes the significance of quantum-design for advanced multi-phase high-entropy alloys with excellent strength-ductility combinations.

Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
